items.subject: MA
items.subskill: comparing fractions one piece short of 1
items.explanation: Each fraction is one piece short of 1 whole: 4/5 is missing 1/5, 5/6 is missing 1/6, 7/8 is missing 1/8 and 9/10 is missing 1/10. Fifths are the biggest pieces, so 4/5 is missing the most and is the smallest.
items.misconceptions: thinks bigger numbers on top and bottom make a bigger fraction, or the reverse

why.B: 5/6 is 1/6 short of a whole, and 1/6 is a smaller piece than 1/5, so 5/6 is closer to 1 than 4/5 is.
why.C: 7/8 is only 1/8 short of a whole, so it is closer to 1, and bigger, than 4/5.
why.D: 9/10 has the biggest numbers, but it is just 1/10 short of a whole: it is the largest of the four, not the smallest.

items.subject: MA
items.subskill: comparing a fraction with one half
items.explanation: A fraction is less than 1/2 when its top number is less than half of its bottom number. Half of 8 is 4, and 3 is less than 4, so 3/8 is less than 1/2.
items.misconceptions: compares only the top numbers or only the bottom numbers

why.B: 6/11 is more than 1/2: half of 11 is 5 1/2, and 6 is more than that.
why.C: 5/9 is more than 1/2: half of 9 is 4 1/2, and 5 is more than that.
why.D: 4/7 is more than 1/2: half of 7 is 3 1/2, and 4 is more than that.

items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

items.subject: MA
items.subskill: a fraction between two benchmarks
items.prompt: Which fraction is greater than 1/3 but less than 1/2?
items.explanation: Check each side. Less than 1/2: half of 5 is 2 1/2, and 2 is less, so 2/5 is under 1/2. More than 1/3: with the same bottom number, 2/5 = 6/15 and 1/3 = 5/15, and 6/15 is more.
items.misconceptions: checks only one side of "between"

why.A: Fourths are smaller pieces than thirds, so 1/4 is less than 1/3.
why.C: 3/5 is more than 1/2: half of 5 is 2 1/2, and 3 is more than that.
why.D: 5/8 is more than 1/2: half of 8 is 4, and 5 is more than 4.

items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

items.subject: MA
items.subskill: comparing fractions with different denominators in a story
items.prompt: Four friends each had a pizza of the same size. Ana ate 2/3 of hers, Leo ate 5/8 of his, Mia ate 3/4 of hers, and Sam ate 7/12 of his. Who ate the most pizza?
items.explanation: Change each amount to a decimal (or to 24ths): 2/3 is about 0.67, 5/8 is 0.625, 3/4 is 0.75 and 7/12 is about 0.58. 3/4 is the largest, so Mia ate the most.
items.misconceptions: picks the fraction with the biggest numbers instead of the biggest value

why.A: Ana ate 2/3, which is 8/12. Mia ate 3/4, which is 9/12, so Mia ate more.
why.B: Leo ate 5/8, which is 0.625. Mia ate 3/4, which is 0.75, so Mia ate more.
why.D: Sam ate 7/12. Mia ate 3/4, which is 9/12, so Mia ate more.

items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

items.subject: MA
items.subskill: writing a decimal as a fraction
items.explanation: 0.45 is 45 hundredths, or 45/100. Divide the top and bottom by 5: 45 ÷ 5 = 9 and 100 ÷ 5 = 20, so 0.45 = 9/20.
items.misconceptions: uses the wrong place value; reads the digits as a fraction

why.A: 45/1000 is 0.045. The 5 in 0.45 is in the hundredths place, so 0.45 is 45/100.
why.C: 4/5 is 0.8. It reads the 4 and the 5 of 0.45 as a top and a bottom number.
why.D: 9/2 is 4 1/2, which is 4.5, ten times too big: 0.45 is 9/20, not 9/2.

items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

items.subject: MA
items.subskill: writing a three-place decimal as a fraction
items.explanation: Know that 1/8 = 0.125 (half of 1/4, which is 0.25). Then 3/8 = 3 × 0.125 = 0.375. Another way: 0.375 is 375/1000, and dividing the top and bottom by 125 gives 3/8.
items.misconceptions: counts the decimal places wrong

why.B: 3/5 is 0.6. It uses only the first digit, 3, and guesses the bottom number.
why.C: 3/4 is 0.75, twice as much as 0.375. 0.375 is half of 0.75, so it is half of 3/4.
why.D: 375/100 is 3.75. 0.375 has three digits after the point, so it is thousandths: 375/1000.

items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

items.subject: MA
items.subskill: writing a fraction as a decimal
items.explanation: Make the bottom number 10: 3/5 = 6/10, and 6 tenths is 0.6.
items.misconceptions: writes the top and bottom digits as a decimal

why.B: 0.35 writes the 3 and the 5 side by side. A fraction bar means divide, not "put the digits together".

items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

items.subject: MA
items.subskill: writing a fraction as a decimal by making 100
items.explanation: Multiply the top and bottom by 4 to make hundredths: 7 × 4 = 28 and 25 × 4 = 100, so 7/25 = 28/100 = 0.28.
items.misconceptions: writes the digits side by side; divides the wrong way

why.A: 0.07 uses only the top number, 7. The bottom number is 25, not 100.
why.C: 0.725 writes the 7 and the 25 side by side. A fraction bar means divide.
why.D: 3.57 is about 25 ÷ 7, the division the wrong way round. 7/25 is less than 1.

items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

items.subject: MA
items.subskill: a decimal between two tenths
items.prompt: Which number is greater than 0.6 and less than 0.7?
items.explanation: Write all the numbers with the same number of places: 0.60, 0.65, 0.70. 0.65 is between 0.60 and 0.70.
items.misconceptions: thinks more digits means a smaller number

why.B: 0.705 is a little more than 0.7, because 0.7 is the same as 0.700.
why.C: 0.76 is more than 0.7, because 0.7 is the same as 0.70.
why.D: 6.5 is six and a half, far more than 0.7. The point is in the wrong place.

items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

items.subject: MA
items.subskill: comparing decimals with different numbers of places
items.explanation: Give every number three places, smallest first: 0.209, 0.250, 0.300, 0.310. Compare the tenths first: 0.250 and 0.209 have 2 tenths, the others 3. Then the hundredths: 0 is less than 5, so 0.209 is the least.
items.misconceptions: thinks the number with fewer digits is smaller

why.B: 0.25 is 0.250, which is more than 0.209: compare the tenths first, then the hundredths.
why.C: 0.3 is 0.300. It has the fewest digits, but 3 tenths is more than 2 tenths.
why.D: 0.31 is 0.310, more than 0.209 and more than 0.3.

items.subject: MA
items.subskill: writing a percent as a fraction
items.explanation: Percent means "out of 100", so 40% = 40/100. Divide the top and bottom by 20: 40/100 = 2/5.
items.misconceptions: misreads "percent" as a place value

why.A: 1/40 is 2.5%. It puts the 40 on the bottom.

items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

items.subject: MA
items.subskill: percent of a number
items.explanation: 25% is one quarter. 36 ÷ 4 = 9.
items.misconceptions: subtracts the percent; uses the wrong fraction

why.B: 11 takes 25 away from 36. 25% means one quarter of 36, not 25 less.
why.C: 12 comes from 36 ÷ 3, which finds a third. 25% is a quarter, so divide by 4.
why.D: 25 copies the percent. 25% of 36 is a part of 36, found by dividing 36 into 4 equal parts.

items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

items.subject: MA
items.subskill: price after a percent discount
items.prompt: A jacket costs $40. It is on sale for 25% off. What is the sale price?
items.explanation: 25% is one quarter. A quarter of $40 is $40 ÷ 4 = $10. The sale price is $40 − $10 = $30.
items.misconceptions: stops at the discount; takes off dollars instead of a percent

why.A: $10 is the amount taken off (25% of $40). The question asks what the jacket costs after that.
why.B: $15 takes 25 dollars off. 25% off means a quarter of the price comes off, and a quarter of $40 is $10.
why.D: $50 adds the $10. "Off" means take it away.

items.subject: MA
items.subskill: writing a part of a group as a percent
items.prompt: There are 20 students in a class, and 12 of them have a pet. What percent of the students have a pet?
items.explanation: 12 out of 20 is 12/20. Multiply the top and bottom by 5 to get hundredths: 60/100 = 60%.
items.misconceptions: uses a count as a percent; finds the other part

why.A: 12% uses the count of students, 12, as if the class had 100 students. It has 20.
why.B: 20% uses the size of the class. The question asks what part of the 20 have a pet.
why.C: 40% is the part without a pet (8 of 20). The question asks about the students who have one.

items.subject: MA
items.subskill: value of a digit
items.prompt: What is the value of the digit 4 in 7,482,036?
items.explanation: In 7,482,036 the 7 is in the millions place and the 4 is in the hundred thousands place, so the 4 is worth 400,000.
items.misconceptions: gives the digit, not its value; miscounts the places

why.A: 4 is the digit itself. The question asks what it is worth where it sits.
why.B: 4,000 is two places too small. Count the places from the right: ones, tens, hundreds, thousands, ten thousands, hundred thousands.
why.C: 40,000 is one place too small. The 4 is in the hundred thousands place.

items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

items.subject: MA
items.subskill: rounding to the nearest thousand
items.prompt: What is 46,751 rounded to the nearest thousand?
items.explanation: Look at the digit one place to the right of the thousands: the hundreds digit, 7. It is 5 or more, so the 6 thousands goes up to 7: 47,000.
items.misconceptions: rounds to the wrong place; rounds down when it should round up

why.A: 46,000 rounds down, but the hundreds digit is 7, which is 5 or more, so round up.
why.B: 46,700 cuts off the last two digits; it is not rounded to a thousand at all.
why.C: 46,800 is 46,751 rounded to the nearest hundred, not the nearest thousand.

items.subject: MA
items.subskill: multi-step problem with regrouping
items.prompt: A school bought 6 boxes of pencils with 144 pencils in each box. It gave out 395 pencils. How many pencils are left?
items.explanation: 6 × 144 = 864 pencils. Then 864 − 395: 14 − 5 = 9 ones, 15 − 9 = 6 tens after regrouping, and 7 − 3 = 4 hundreds. 469 pencils are left.
items.misconceptions: loses a regrouped digit; adds instead of subtracting

why.A: 325 uses 5 boxes (5 × 144 = 720). The school bought 6 boxes, 864 pencils.
why.C: 579 regroups but never takes away what it borrowed: after lending, the 6 tens become 5 and the 8 hundreds become 7.
why.D: 1,259 adds the 395 pencils. They were given out, so take them away.

items.subject: MA
items.subskill: what a remainder means in a story
items.prompt: Ninety-two students are going on a trip. Each van holds 8 students. What is the least number of vans needed?
items.explanation: 92 ÷ 8 = 11 with 4 left over. Eleven vans hold 88 students, and the other 4 need a twelfth van, so 12 vans.
items.misconceptions: drops the remainder instead of adding one more group

why.A: 4 is the remainder: 92 = 11 × 8 + 4. Those 4 students still need a van.
why.B: 11 vans hold 88 students, so 4 students would be left behind. They need one more van.
why.D: 100 adds 92 and 8. Sharing students into vans is division.

items.subject: MA
items.subskill: common multiples
items.prompt: Which number is a multiple of both 6 and 8?
items.explanation: Count by 8s and check each for 6: 8, 16, 24 — 24 is 6 × 4. The multiples of both are 24, 48, 72 … and 48 = 6 × 8.
items.misconceptions: adds the numbers; checks only one of them

why.A: 14 is 6 + 8. A multiple of 6 is in the 6 times table, and 14 is not.
why.B: 32 is a multiple of 8 (4 × 8) but not of 6.
why.C: 36 is a multiple of 6 (6 × 6) but not of 8.

items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

items.subject: MA
items.subskill: estimating a product
items.prompt: Which is the best estimate of 412 × 49?
items.explanation: Round each number to one it is close to: 412 is about 400 and 49 is about 50. 400 × 50 = 20,000.
items.misconceptions: loses or adds a zero; rounds to a far number

why.A: 2,000 drops a zero: 400 × 50 has three zeros in all.
why.C: 25,000 rounds 412 up to 500, but 412 is much closer to 400.
why.D: 200,000 adds an extra zero: 4 × 5 = 20, then 400 × 50 = 20 with three zeros.

items.subject: MA
items.subskill: fraction of a whole number
items.explanation: Split 28 into 4 equal parts: 28 ÷ 4 = 7. Three of those parts are 3 × 7 = 21.
items.misconceptions: stops at one part; multiplies by the bottom number

why.A: 7 comes from 28 ÷ 4, just one quarter. 3/4 is three of those quarters: 3 × 7.
why.B: 14 comes from 28 ÷ 2, a half. 3/4 is more than a half.
why.D: 112 is 28 × 4. Finding 3/4 of a number makes it smaller.

items.subject: MA
items.subskill: adding fractions with different denominators
items.explanation: Make sixths: 2/3 = 4/6. Then 4/6 + 1/6 = 5/6.
items.misconceptions: adds tops and bottoms; subtracts

why.A: 3/18 adds the top numbers and multiplies the bottom ones. Make the bottom numbers the same first.
why.B: 3/9 adds the top numbers and the bottom numbers. Only the top numbers are added, once the bottoms match.
why.C: 1/2 is 2/3 − 1/6, a subtraction. The question adds.

items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

items.subject: MA
items.subskill: mixed number to improper fraction
items.explanation: Each whole is 5 fifths, so 2 wholes are 10 fifths. Add the 3 fifths: 10 + 3 = 13. 2 3/5 = 13/5.
items.misconceptions: multiplies the wrong numbers; writes digits side by side

why.A: 11/5 multiplies 2 × 3 and adds 5. Multiply the whole number by the bottom number: 2 × 5 = 10, then add 3.
why.C: 23/5 writes the 2 and 3 side by side. 2 wholes are 10 fifths, not 20.
why.D: 30/5 multiplies all three numbers. 30/5 is 6, much more than 2 3/5.

items.subject: MA
items.subskill: adding decimals by lining up the points
items.explanation: Line up the decimal points and write 3.6 as 3.60. Then 3.60 + 0.45 = 4.05.
items.misconceptions: lines up digits instead of decimal points

why.A: 0.81 lines up the last digits (36 + 45) instead of the decimal points.
why.B: 3.65 adds only the 5 hundredths and forgets the 4 tenths.
why.D: 8.1 lines up the first digits (3.6 + 4.5). The 4 in 0.45 is 4 tenths, so it goes under the 6.
